title: Mastering the Jones Tube: Conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy (CDCR)
summary: The definitive surgical bypass procedure for proximal lacrimal system failure. CDCR utilizes a Pyrex Jones tube to create a direct conduit from the lacrimal lake to the middle meatus when canalicular function is irrecoverable.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy (CDCR) is a bypass surgery of the upper lacrimal drainage system. It involves the permanent placement of a prosthetic tube (usually a Pyrex glass Jones tube) extending from the medial canthus (lacrimal lake) directly into the nasal cavity. It is indicated when the natural canalicular system is absent, obliterated, or severely dysfunctional (<8mm of patent canaliculus remaining).

sections.title: Mandatory Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. Dye Disappearance Test (DDT): Assess functional tear clearance.
2. Lacrimal Probing: Determine the exact site and length of canalicular obstruction.
3. Diagnostic Irrigation: Confirm total vs. partial block (Hard vs. Soft stop).
4. Nasal Endoscopy: Rule out septal deviation or turbinate hypertrophy that may obstruct tube exit.
5. Schirmer Test: Ensure adequate tear production (Dry eye patients tolerate tubes poorly).

sections.title: Surgical Technique: Step-by-Step
content: Step 1: Standard DCR approach (External or Endoscopic) to create an osteotomy (approx 15mm diameter).
Step 2: Excision of the caruncle to create a raw bed for the tube collar.
Step 3: Insertion of a 22-gauge MVR blade or 14-gauge needle from the caruncle bed towards the osteotomy, angled 45° inferiorly and medially.
Step 4: Dilation of the tract using a Bowman probe or specialized trephine.
Step 5: Tube Sizing: Measure the distance from the caruncle to the nasal cavity. Ensure the distal end is 2-3mm away from the nasal septum.
Step 6: Tube Insertion: Slide the Pyrex tube over a guide wire (usually a Supramid suture or Bowman probe).
Step 7: Fixation: A 6-0 Prolene suture is passed around the tube neck and secured to the medial canthal tendon.
Step 8: Closure: Standard closure of DCR flaps and skin if external approach was used.

sections.title: Contraindications & Red Flags
content: Severe Dry Eye Disease (Tube increases evaporation and irritates ocular surface)
Active Dacryocystitis or Sinusitis
Psychiatric conditions/Dementia (Risk of self-mutilation or poor hygiene)
Nasal Cocaine Abuse (Septal necrosis/poor healing)
Bleeding Diathesis (high vascularity of nasal mucosa)

sections.title: Post-Operative Maintenance
content: Frequent 'Sniffing' of saline drops to clear mucus plugs.
Valsalva maneuver (with eyes closed) to clear debris.
Nasal steroid sprays if granulation tissue forms.
Annual professional cleaning (tube removal and ultrasound bath if calcified).
Teach patient to keep eyes closed when sneezing to prevent 'Tube Projectile'.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The 'Golden Rule': The distal end of the tube must be visible in the middle meatus and 2mm clear of the septum.
If the tube is too short, it will migrate into the ethmoid air cells.
A 'Sniff Test' in the office: If the patient can draw saline from the medial canthus into the throat, the tube is patent.
Canalicular reconstructive surgery should always be attempted before CDCR if >8mm of canaliculus is healthy.

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Insights
sections.content: The original Lester Jones paper (1962) emphasized the use of Pyrex due to its high 'wettability' and capillary action. Modern series (e.g., Rose et al.) show that while initial success is high (>90%), long-term maintenance is required for life, with up to 50% of patients requiring at least one tube replacement or repositioning over 10 years.

sections.title: Pediatric CDCR Considerations
content: Rarely indicated; reserved for severe congenital agenesis.
General anesthesia required for all revisions/cleaning.
Growth of the midface may necessitate tube length changes over time.
Higher risk of accidental extrusion during play.
